BULK SALE NOTICE WHEN A BUSINESS'S INVENTORY IS SOLD (CAL. U. COM. CODE §§ 6101–6111; GIFFORD V. J & A HOLDINGS; MONASTRA V. KONICA BUSINESS MACHINES; BUS. & PROF. CODE § 24074) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Pat Morgan

PURPOSE AND SCOPE — CALIFORNIA BULK SALE NOTICE INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet concerns the sale of the business known as Acme, Inc. by Pat Morgan to Jordan Lee, recorded here as closing on November 15, 2026. It describes California's bulk sale law — Division 6 of the Commercial Code, sections 6101 through 6111 — which requires the buyer in certain sales of a business's inventory and equipment to record, publish, and send a public notice before the sale, and in certain smaller cash sales to route the purchase money through a claims procedure for the seller's creditors. It sets out the statute's definition of a bulk sale, the two conditions that bring a sale within the division, the sixteen categories of excluded transactions, who counts as a "claimant," the buyer's three statutory duties, the required contents of the notice and the 12-business-day recording and publication deadline (and the Court of Appeal's holding in Gifford v. J & A Holdings on how that deadline is measured), the escrow claims procedure for sales of $2,000,000 or less that are substantially all cash, the priority order when the money is not enough to pay every claim, what a buyer's noncompliance does and does not cost the buyer, the good-faith and commercially-reasonable-effort defense, the rules for auctions and liquidators, the one-year limitation period, the Court of Appeal's holding in Monastra v. Konica Business Machines that compliance with the bulk sale law does not immunize a transfer from attack under the fraudulent transfer laws, and the separate alcoholic-beverage-license escrow that Business and Professions Code section 24074 requires. Whether the sale of Acme, Inc. is a bulk sale within the meaning of the statute, whether Pat Morgan's principal business is the sale of inventory from stock or that of a restaurant owner, what Jordan Lee did or did not record, publish, or send, what the assets were worth, and who the seller's creditors are, are all facts this sheet does not determine. Naming the parties and a closing date here does not itself establish that any rule described below applies to this transaction, and this sheet states what the statutes and the courts say rather than advising anyone what to do about a particular sale, claim, or defense.

WHAT A "BULK SALE" IS, AND THE TWO CONDITIONS THAT BRING A SALE WITHIN DIVISION 6
California's bulk sale law is Division 6 of the Commercial Code. Section 6101 states that the division may be cited as Uniform Commercial Code—Bulk Sales. Outside the auction and liquidator setting, section 6102(a)(3)(ii) defines a bulk sale as a sale not in the ordinary course of the seller's business of more than half the seller's inventory and equipment, measured by value on the date of the bulk-sale agreement. Two other definitions supply the measuring rods: "value" means fair market value, and a sale is "in the ordinary course of the seller's business" if it comports with usual or customary practices in the kind of business the seller is in or with the seller's own usual or customary practices. Meeting that definition is not by itself enough to bring a sale within the division. Section 6103(a) adds two conditions that must both be satisfied: the seller's principal business must be the sale of inventory from stock, including those who manufacture what they sell, or that of a restaurant owner; and on the date of the bulk-sale agreement the seller must be located in this state, or, if the seller is located outside the United States, its major United States executive office must be here. Section 6103(b) locates the seller at its place of business, or at its chief executive office if it has more than one. A separate defined term, the "date of the bulk sale," fixes the point from which the statute's deadlines and its limitation period run: in the ordinary (non-auction) case it is the later of the date on which more than 10 percent of the net contract price is paid to or for the benefit of the seller and the date on which more than 10 percent of the assets, measured by value, are transferred to the buyer.

THE SIXTEEN CATEGORIES OF TRANSACTIONS DIVISION 6 DOES NOT REACH, INCLUDING THE $10,000 FLOOR AND $5,000,000 CEILING
Section 6103(c) lists sixteen categories of transactions to which the division does not apply, even where the definition of a bulk sale and the two conditions of section 6103(a) are otherwise met. Two of them are dollar limits at either end: the division does not reach a sale of assets whose value, net of liens and security interests, is less than ten thousand dollars, and it does not reach a sale of assets whose value is more than five million dollars on the date of the bulk-sale agreement. For those limits, section 6103(f) presumes the value of the assets equals the price the buyer agrees to pay, except in an auction or liquidation sale, where the presumed value is the auctioneer's or liquidator's reasonable estimate of what the assets will bring. Three further exclusions turn on the buyer assuming the seller's debts: a buyer that obtains a verified list of claimants (or conducts a reasonable inquiry), assumes in full the debts owed to claimants it knows of, remains solvent after the assumption, and records and publishes notice of the assumption within 30 days after the bulk sale; a buyer that assumes in full all debts incurred in the seller's business before the bulk sale, remains solvent, and records and publishes the same notice; and a new organization formed to take over and continue the seller's business, where it assumes those debts, the seller receives nothing but a subordinated interest in the new organization, and the notice is likewise recorded and published. Section 6103(d) and (e) prescribe what those after-the-fact assumption notices must say. The remaining exclusions cover security transfers and enforcement of security interests, sales of encumbered assets where all proceeds go to the secured debt or the net contract price is zero, general assignments for the benefit of creditors, sales by an executor, administrator, receiver, trustee in bankruptcy, debtor in possession, or public officer under judicial process, sales in dissolution or reorganization proceedings, sales required by and made pursuant to statute, certain sale-leasebacks complying with Civil Code section 3440.1, transfers of alcoholic beverage licenses that comply with the Business and Professions Code escrow article, and transfers of warehoused goods covered by a warehouse receipt.

WHO COUNTS AS A "CLAIMANT": THE CREDITORS THE DIVISION PROTECTS, AND THE THREE EXCLUDED KINDS OF CLAIMS
The buyer's liability under Division 6 runs to "claimants," a term the statute defines more narrowly than "creditor." A "claim" is a right to payment from the seller, whether or not reduced to judgment, liquidated, fixed, matured, disputed, secured, legal, or equitable, and it includes costs of collection and attorney's fees only so far as California law would let the holder recover them from the obligor. A "creditor" is a claimant or other person holding a claim. A "claimant" is a person holding a claim incurred in the seller's business, but the definition excludes three kinds of claims. The first is an unsecured and unmatured claim for employment compensation and benefits, including commissions and vacation, severance, and sick-leave pay. The second is a claim for injury to an individual or to property, or for breach of warranty, unless a right of action has accrued, the claim has been asserted against the seller, and the seller knows who is asserting it and on what basis. The third is a claim for taxes owing to a governmental unit where a statute governing enforcement of that claim permits or requires notice of the bulk sale to be given in some manner other than by complying with Division 6, and notice is given in accordance with that statute.

THE BUYER'S THREE STATUTORY DUTIES
Section 6104 places the duties of compliance on the buyer, not the seller. In a bulk sale as defined in section 6102(a)(3)(ii) — that is, in every case except a sale by auction or a sale conducted by a liquidator on the seller's behalf — the buyer must do three things. First, obtain from the seller a list of all business names and addresses the seller used within three years before the date the list is sent or delivered to the buyer; that list feeds the notice, which must identify the seller's other business names. Second, give notice of the bulk sale in accordance with section 6105. Third, comply with section 6106.2 if the bulk sale is within the scope of that section, which is the claims-and-escrow procedure for sales of two million dollars or less that are substantially all cash. Section 6107, taken up in a later clause, measures a buyer's liability by its failure to comply with the requirements of section 6104, so all three duties are the measure of compliance.

WHAT THE NOTICE MUST SAY, WHERE IT MUST BE RECORDED AND PUBLISHED, AND THE 12-BUSINESS-DAY DEADLINE
Section 6105 governs the notice itself. The notice must state that a bulk sale is about to be made; the name and business address of the seller together with any other business name and address on the list the buyer obtained under section 6104(a), and the name and business address of the buyer; the location and general description of the assets; the place and the anticipated date of the bulk sale; and whether the sale is subject to section 6106.2, adding, if it is, the claim-filing information that section requires. The notice must then be put in three places at least 12 business days before the date of the bulk sale. It must be recorded in the office of the county recorder in each California county where the tangible assets are located and, if different, in the county where the seller is located. It must be published at least once in a newspaper of general circulation published in the public notice district where the tangible assets are located and, if different, in the district where the seller is located, with a rule for choosing among districts when the assets are spread across more than one. And it must be delivered or sent by registered or certified mail to the county tax collector in each California county where the tangible assets are located; a notice delivered between January 1 and May 7 must be accompanied by a completed business property statement under Revenue and Taxation Code section 441. For this section, publication in a public notice district is governed by the Government Code, and "business day" means any day other than a Saturday, Sunday, or day observed as a holiday by the state government.

HOW THE 12-BUSINESS-DAY PERIOD IS MEASURED: GIFFORD V. J & A HOLDINGS
Section 6105(a)(4) requires the notice to state the "anticipated date" of the bulk sale, while section 6105(b) requires recording and publication at least 12 business days before "the date of the bulk sale," a term section 6102(a)(7) defines by reference to payment and transfer. In Gifford v. J & A Holdings (1997), the buyer of a restaurant business recorded the notice fewer than 12 business days before the anticipated sale date stated in the notice, then postponed the close of escrow so that 12 business days passed before the sale actually closed; a produce supplier who never filed a claim sued. The trial court read the statute literally and found compliance. The Court of Appeal reversed, treating the timeliness of the recording as a question of law for its independent review. It reasoned that the purpose of the scheme is to protect creditors by giving them notice in time to act before the transfer, and that the notice date determines the claim-filing deadline, since section 6106.2(f) makes the last day for filing claims the business day before the anticipated date stated in the notice. Reading section 6105(b) in that light, the court held that the notice must be published and recorded at least 12 business days before the anticipated sale date as specified in the notice, because otherwise creditors do not have sufficient time to file a timely claim. THE CLAIMS PROCEDURE FOR BULK SALES OF $2,000,000 OR LESS THAT ARE SUBSTANTIALLY ALL CASH
Section 6106.2 adds a second layer of obligation to certain smaller sales. It applies only where the consideration is two million dollars or less and is substantially all cash, or an obligation of the buyer to pay cash in the future, or a combination of the two. In such a sale (other than an auction or liquidator sale), the buyer — or the escrow agent, if the transaction is handled through escrow — has a duty to apply the cash consideration so far as necessary to pay the seller's debts for which claims are due and payable on or before the date of the bulk sale and are received in writing by the claim-filing deadline, and that duty runs to each claimant who files timely. The notice for such a sale must state, in addition to what section 6105 requires, the name and address of the person with whom claims may be filed and the last date for filing claims, which is the business day before the anticipated sale date stated in the notice; a claim counts as timely only if actually received by that person before the close of business on that day. Within 45 days after the buyer takes legal title to any of the goods, the buyer or escrow agent must either pay the undisputed filed claims to the extent of the cash consideration or file an interpleader action and deposit the consideration with the clerk of the court. If the seller disputes whether a claim is due and payable or disputes its amount, the buyer or escrow agent must withhold 125 percent of the first $7,500 of the claim plus the balance of the claim (or the pro rata amount under section 6106.4), notify the claimant, and pay the withheld money out unless the claimant attaches it within 25 days of the mailing of that notice. Complying with this section does not release any security interest or other lien on the property sold except by the lienholder's voluntary release.

WHEN THE PURCHASE MONEY IS NOT ENOUGH: DEPOSIT, DELAY, NOTICE, AND THE STATUTORY ORDER OF PAYMENT
Section 6106.4 governs the case where the money runs short. Where the notice states that claims may be filed with an escrow agent, the intended buyer must deposit the full amount of the purchase price or consideration with that agent. If, when the sale is otherwise ready to close, the cash in escrow is not enough to pay all filed claims in full, the escrow agent must delay distribution of the consideration and the passing of legal title for not less than 25 and not more than 30 days from the mailing of a notice; must send that notice within five business days after the sale would otherwise have closed, stating the total consideration, the name and amount of every claim filed, the amount proposed to be paid on each, the new title-passing date, and the date distribution will be made; and, if no written objection arrives before the new title-passing date, is shielded from liability to the noticed claimants for any good faith error in allocating and distributing the money. The consideration is then distributed in a fixed order: obligations owing to the United States to the extent federal law gives them priority; secured claims, including statutory and judicial liens, to the extent of the consideration fairly attributable to the value of the security, and only if the secured creditor deposits a release of lien; escrow and professional charges and brokers' fees attributable directly to the sale; wage claims given priority by Code of Civil Procedure section 1205; all other tax claims; and finally all other unsecured claims pro rata, including deficiency claims of partially secured creditors. Where part of the consideration is the buyer's obligation to pay cash in the future and the cash is insufficient, all principal and interest received on that obligation goes to the claims in the same order until they are paid in full before anything is paid to the seller.

WHAT NONCOMPLIANCE COSTS THE BUYER — AND WHAT IT DOES NOT DO TO THE SALE
Section 6107 states the consequence of a buyer's failure to comply with section 6104. Subject to the good-faith defense and the liability cap, a noncomplying buyer is liable to a claimant for damages in the amount of the claim, reduced by any amount the claimant would not have realized had the buyer complied. The burdens are split: the claimant must establish the validity and amount of the claim, and the buyer must establish the amount the claimant would not have realized. The buyer's cumulative liability in a single bulk sale is capped — where the assets are only inventory and equipment, at twice the net contract price, less amounts of that price already paid to or applied for the benefit of the seller or a creditor, with an exception for payments applied to debts secured by the assets and already taken into account in computing the net contract price; where the assets include other property, a parallel cap is set at twice the net value of the inventory and equipment. No action lies on behalf of a claimant whose claim is unliquidated or contingent, and payments the buyer makes reduce the cumulative cap pro tanto. The statute is equally explicit about what noncompliance does not do: it does not impair the buyer's rights in or title to the assets, does not render the sale ineffective, void, or voidable, does not entitle a creditor to more than a single satisfaction of its claim, and does not create liability other than as provided in the division. Payment of the buyer's liability discharges the seller's debt to that creditor pro tanto, and unless otherwise agreed the buyer has an immediate right of reimbursement from the seller for whatever it pays.

THE GOOD-FAITH, COMMERCIALLY-REASONABLE-EFFORT DEFENSE, AND HOW GIFFORD APPLIED IT
Section 6107(c) gives a noncomplying buyer a defense: a buyer who made a good faith and commercially reasonable effort to comply with section 6104, or to exclude the sale from the division under section 6103(c), is not liable to creditors for the failure to comply, and the buyer carries the burden of establishing the good faith and commercial reasonableness of the effort. In Gifford v. J & A Holdings the trial court found that defense satisfied because the purchase agreement and escrow instructions expressed an intent to comply and because postponing the escrow amounted to substantial compliance. The Court of Appeal disagreed. It observed that commercial reasonableness is not expressly defined in the statute but has been defined elsewhere to include commonly accepted commercial practices of responsible businesses that afford all parties fair treatment, and that good faith and commercial reasonableness are primarily questions of fact reviewed for substantial evidence. On the record before it the court found no substantial evidence of such an effort: curing an untimely recording merely by postponing the close of escrow does not address the substance of the statute's objective of giving creditors time to file a claim before the date specified in the notice, and the buyer, knowing the notice was untimely and knowing the identity of the seller's major creditor, neither recorded a new notice nor gave that creditor actual notice. The court also rejected the argument that a late claim would have been honored anyway, noting that a creditor who learns the stated filing deadline has passed should conclude, especially after reading section 6106.2(b) and (f), that filing a late claim would be useless.

Section 6110 sets the time limit for suing under the division. COMPLIANCE WITH THE BULK SALE LAW DOES NOT IMMUNIZE THE TRANSFER FROM THE FRAUDULENT TRANSFER LAWS: MONASTRA V. KONICA BUSINESS MACHINES
In Monastra v. Konica Business Machines, U.S.A., Inc. (1996), a judgment creditor of a business sued the buyers of its assets, alleging fraudulent transfer, conspiracy, and a constructive trust. The buyers answered that they had complied with the bulk sale law and that compliance insulated the sale from any other attack; the trial court agreed and granted summary judgment. The Court of Appeal reversed, calling the question one of first impression and holding that the Bulk Sales Act and the fraudulent transfer laws represent cumulative independent statutory schemes, and that compliance with one does not satisfy the requirements of the other. Discussing the purpose of the bulk sale scheme, the court described the central purpose of the bulk sales statutes as affording a merchant's creditors an opportunity to satisfy their claims before the merchant can transfer his or her assets and vanish with the sale proceeds, and emphasized the word "before": the article is designed to enable creditors to protect themselves before a bulk sale rather than to seek whatever remedy may remain afterward. But the court distinguished the adequacy of recorded and published notice for that purpose from the idea that such notice is all the protection creditors need against those who would willfully cheat them. Because the defendants had not denied the plaintiff's factual claims and relied solely on the immunity argument the court rejected, triable issues remained on the fraudulent transfer claims.

The notice must state that a bulk sale is about to be made; the name and business address of the seller together with any other business name and address on the list the buyer obtained under section 6104(a), and the name and business address of the buyer; the location and general description of the assets; the place and the anticipated date of the bulk sale; and whether the sale is subject to section 6106.2, adding, if it is, the claim-filing information that section requires. It must be published at least once in a newspaper of general circulation published in the public notice district where the tangible assets are located and, if different, in the district where the seller is located, with a rule for choosing among districts when the assets are spread across more than one. And it must be delivered or sent by registered or certified mail to the county tax collector in each California county where the tangible assets are located; a notice delivered between January 1 and May 7 must be accompanied by a completed business property statement under Revenue and Taxation Code section 441. For this section, publication in a public notice district is governed by the Government Code, and "business day" means any day other than a Saturday, Sunday, or day observed as a holiday by the state government.

In Gifford v. J & A Holdings (1997), the buyer of a restaurant business recorded the notice fewer than 12 business days before the anticipated sale date stated in the notice, then postponed the close of escrow so that 12 business days passed before the sale actually closed; a produce supplier who never filed a claim sued. The trial court read the statute literally and found compliance. The Court of Appeal reversed, treating the timeliness of the recording as a question of law for its independent review. It reasoned that the purpose of the scheme is to protect creditors by giving them notice in time to act before the transfer, and that the notice date determines the claim-filing deadline, since section 6106.2(f) makes the last day for filing claims the business day before the anticipated date stated in the notice. Reading section 6105(b) in that light, the court held that the notice must be published and recorded at least 12 business days before the anticipated sale date as specified in the notice, because otherwise creditors do not have sufficient time to file a timely claim. The court added a limit to its holding: a new notice need not be published and recorded every time the anticipated date of sale is postponed by glitches in the escrow process; what the holding requires is 12 business days before the date the notice itself specifies as the anticipated date of sale, because that specification sets the last day for filing claims.

expectedJSON.body: Section 6106.2 adds a second layer of obligation to certain smaller sales. It applies only where the consideration is two million dollars or less and is substantially all cash, or an obligation of the buyer to pay cash in the future, or a combination of the two. In such a sale (other than an auction or liquidator sale), the buyer — or the escrow agent, if the transaction is handled through escrow — has a duty to apply the cash consideration so far as necessary to pay the seller's debts for which claims are due and payable on or before the date of the bulk sale and are received in writing by the claim-filing deadline, and that duty runs to each claimant who files timely. The notice for such a sale must state, in addition to what section 6105 requires, the name and address of the person with whom claims may be filed and the last date for filing claims, which is the business day before the anticipated sale date stated in the notice; a claim counts as timely only if actually received by that person before the close of business on that day. Within 45 days after the buyer takes legal title to any of the goods, the buyer or escrow agent must either pay the undisputed filed claims to the extent of the cash consideration or file an interpleader action and deposit the consideration with the clerk of the court. If the seller disputes whether a claim is due and payable or disputes its amount, the buyer or escrow agent must withhold 125 percent of the first $7,500 of the claim plus the balance of the claim (or the pro rata amount under section 6106.4), notify the claimant, and pay the withheld money out unless the claimant attaches it within 25 days of the mailing of that notice. Complying with this section does not release any security interest or other lien on the property sold except by the lienholder's voluntary release.

expectedJSON.body: Section 6106.4 governs the case where the money runs short. Where the notice states that claims may be filed with an escrow agent, the intended buyer must deposit the full amount of the purchase price or consideration with that agent. If, when the sale is otherwise ready to close, the cash in escrow is not enough to pay all filed claims in full, the escrow agent must delay distribution of the consideration and the passing of legal title for not less than 25 and not more than 30 days from the mailing of a notice; must send that notice within five business days after the sale would otherwise have closed, stating the total consideration, the name and amount of every claim filed, the amount proposed to be paid on each, the new title-passing date, and the date distribution will be made; and, if no written objection arrives before the new title-passing date, is shielded from liability to the noticed claimants for any good faith error in allocating and distributing the money. The consideration is then distributed in a fixed order: obligations owing to the United States to the extent federal law gives them priority; secured claims, including statutory and judicial liens, to the extent of the consideration fairly attributable to the value of the security, and only if the secured creditor deposits a release of lien; escrow and professional charges and brokers' fees attributable directly to the sale; wage claims given priority by Code of Civil Procedure section 1205; all other tax claims; and finally all other unsecured claims pro rata, including deficiency claims of partially secured creditors. Where part of the consideration is the buyer's obligation to pay cash in the future and the cash is insufficient, all principal and interest received on that obligation goes to the claims in the same order until they are paid in full before anything is paid to the seller.

expectedJSON.body: Section 6107 states the consequence of a buyer's failure to comply with section 6104. Subject to the good-faith defense and the liability cap, a noncomplying buyer is liable to a claimant for damages in the amount of the claim, reduced by any amount the claimant would not have realized had the buyer complied. The burdens are split: the claimant must establish the validity and amount of the claim, and the buyer must establish the amount the claimant would not have realized. The buyer's cumulative liability in a single bulk sale is capped — where the assets are only inventory and equipment, at twice the net contract price, less amounts of that price already paid to or applied for the benefit of the seller or a creditor, with an exception for payments applied to debts secured by the assets and already taken into account in computing the net contract price; where the assets include other property, a parallel cap is set at twice the net value of the inventory and equipment. No action lies on behalf of a claimant whose claim is unliquidated or contingent, and payments the buyer makes reduce the cumulative cap pro tanto. The statute is equally explicit about what noncompliance does not do: it does not impair the buyer's rights in or title to the assets, does not render the sale ineffective, void, or voidable, does not entitle a creditor to more than a single satisfaction of its claim, and does not create liability other than as provided in the division. Payment of the buyer's liability discharges the seller's debt to that creditor pro tanto, and unless otherwise agreed the buyer has an immediate right of reimbursement from the seller for whatever it pays.

The Court of Appeal disagreed. It observed that commercial reasonableness is not expressly defined in the statute but has been defined elsewhere to include commonly accepted commercial practices of responsible businesses that afford all parties fair treatment, and that good faith and commercial reasonableness are primarily questions of fact reviewed for substantial evidence. On the record before it the court found no substantial evidence of such an effort: curing an untimely recording merely by postponing the close of escrow does not address the substance of the statute's objective of giving creditors time to file a claim before the date specified in the notice, and the buyer, knowing the notice was untimely and knowing the identity of the seller's major creditor, neither recorded a new notice nor gave that creditor actual notice. The court also rejected the argument that a late claim would have been honored anyway, noting that a creditor who learns the stated filing deadline has passed should conclude, especially after reading section 6106.2(b) and (f), that filing a late claim would be useless.

expectedJSON.body: Section 6110 sets the time limit for suing under the division. An action against a buyer, auctioneer, or liquidator must be commenced within one year after the date of the bulk sale — the date fixed by the definitions in section 6102(a)(7), not the date of the contract. The one exception is concealment: if the buyer, auctioneer, or liquidator conceals the fact that the sale has occurred, the limitation is tolled, and the action may be brought within the earlier of one year after the person bringing the action discovers the sale and one year after that person should have discovered it, but in no event later than two years after the date of the bulk sale. The statute forecloses one reading of that exception in terms: complete noncompliance with the requirements of the division does not of itself constitute concealment.

expectedJSON.body: In Monastra v. Konica Business Machines, U.S.A., Inc. (1996), a judgment creditor of a business sued the buyers of its assets, alleging fraudulent transfer, conspiracy, and a constructive trust. The buyers answered that they had complied with the bulk sale law and that compliance insulated the sale from any other attack; the trial court agreed and granted summary judgment. The Court of Appeal reversed, calling the question one of first impression and holding that the Bulk Sales Act and the fraudulent transfer laws represent cumulative independent statutory schemes, and that compliance with one does not satisfy the requirements of the other. Discussing the purpose of the bulk sale scheme, the court described the central purpose of the bulk sales statutes as affording a merchant's creditors an opportunity to satisfy their claims before the merchant can transfer his or her assets and vanish with the sale proceeds, and emphasized the word "before": the article is designed to enable creditors to protect themselves before a bulk sale rather than to seek whatever remedy may remain afterward. But the court distinguished the adequacy of recorded and published notice for that purpose from the idea that such notice is all the protection creditors need against those who would willfully cheat them. Because the defendants had not denied the plaintiff's factual claims and relied solely on the immunity argument the court rejected, triable issues remained on the fraudulent transfer claims.

expectedJSON.body: A bulk sale of a restaurant, bar, or store that holds an alcoholic beverage license may be governed by a different creditor-protection statute. Section 6103(c)(15) excludes from Division 6 a transfer that is subject to and complies with the license-transfer article of the Business and Professions Code (Article 5, commencing with section 24070), provided the transferee records and publishes notice of the transfer at least 12 business days before the transfer is consummated in the manner section 6105 provides, and the notice contains the information required by paragraphs (1) through (4) of section 6105(a). That article's core provision, section 24074, requires that before a transfer application is filed with the Department of Alcoholic Beverage Control, if the transfer involves a purchase price or consideration, the licensee and the intended transferee must establish an escrow with a person not a party to the transfer and the transferee must deposit the full amount of the purchase price with the escrow holder; the application must be accompanied by a description of the entire consideration, designating cash, checks, promissory notes, and tangible and intangible property. The parties must also sign an agreement, deposited with the escrow holder, directing it to pay the claims of bona fide creditors who file before the department notifies the escrow holder of its approval of the license transfer, and, if the consideration is insufficient, to distribute it in an eight-step statutory order that begins with federal income and withholding tax claims and other tax claims, then employee wage, salary, and fringe benefit claims accrued before the sale, then secured creditors to the extent of their security, then mechanics' liens, then escrow fees and prevailing brokerage and reasonable attorney's fees, then claims for goods sold and delivered for resale at the licensed premises, services connected with the business, and a landlord's past-due rent, then court-ordered judgments including child support, and finally all other claims, pro rata if the assets are insufficient. If the transferor disputes a claim, the escrow holder notifies the claimant and holds the amount for 25 days, paying it to the transferor if it is not attached.

citations.quote: If the transferor licensee disputes any claim, the escrow holder shall notify the claimant, and the amount or pro rata amount thereof shall be retained by the escrow holder for a period of 25 days, and if not attached shall be paid to the transferor licensee.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause describes the intersection of two statutes; it does not state that any particular sale of a licensed business falls under one rather than the other. Section 6103(c)(15) removes a transfer from Division 6 only if the transfer is subject to and complies with the Business and Professions Code article and the transferee also records and publishes the section 6105 notice at least 12 business days before consummation with the information required by section 6105(a)(1) through (4); a transfer that satisfies neither statute is outside the scope of both exclusions. Section 24074 is quoted in part: its opening escrow and deposit requirement and its disputed-claim provision are quoted, while the eight priority categories are summarized in the clause body from the statutory list. The rest of Article 5 (including sections 24071, 24073, and 24074.1 through 24082, and the requirements of section 24049 the escrow agreement refers to) was not fetched for this sheet, and the Department of Alcoholic Beverage Control's own transfer procedures are not described.
